To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the mechanical splenic retention in vitro of ring-infected erythrocytes from subjects with normal HbAA or sickle-cell trait (HBA/HbS) does not differ, and that the retention of ring-infested erythrocytes in the spleen is not associated with the sickling phenotype.
the spleen retains sickle-cell trait red blood cells (HbAS), but the retention of ring-infested cells is the same as that of normal red blood cells (i.e. HbAA).
sickle-cell trait is not a mechanism for the protection against malaria in children.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanical sensing of malaria-infected RBC in the spleen.
the role of the spleen in malaria and sickle cell anaemia.
the mechanisms that underlie protection from falciparum infection conferred by sickle-cell trait.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the spleen-dependent clearance of ring-stage infected red blood cells is not the mechanism that accounts for the reduced risk of severe malaria in individuals with sickle-cell trait.
sickling of ring stage infected red blood cells is not a major mechanism for protection of HbAS against malaria.

sickle-cell trait is not protective against malaria because it enhances the mechanical splenic removal of ring-infector RBCs, as previously suggested, but because it impairs the cytoadhesion of mature parasites to endothelial cells, thus reducing the splenic sequestration of mature infected RBCs.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the spleen is not a major site for the protection against malaria conferred by sickle-cell trait.
sickle-cell trait is not protective against P. falcipaurum infection by reducing the mechanical splenic retention or the sickling of ring-stage infected red blood cells.
the spleen-dependent removal and clearance of ring-infected erythrocytes is not affected by sickle-cell trait.
The main takeaway from our work is that
sickle-cell trait is unlikely to be a major determinant of the lower parasitaemian and the delayed malaria episodes observed in sickle-cell carriers.
sickle cell trait does not protect by increasing splenic clearance of ring stage-infected red blood cell, but rather by impairing the cytoadhesion of infected red blood cell.
the spleen is an efficient filter for mature parasites, which may be the main factor explaining why HbAS individuals do not develop severe malaria.
